scenario: Middle-aged man with exertional chest pain radiating to the left arm; possible angina; sent to hospital.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Good evening, Mohan. You look a bit tired. What is the problem?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Good evening, doctor. Sorry, the lift is not working in your building, I had to climb three floors. Doctor, I have this chest pain. It comes when I walk fast or climb the stairs.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Tell me about the pain. Where exactly, and what does it feel like?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: In the middle of the chest, like a heavy weight, tight. And it goes down my left arm, and sometimes to the jaw.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How long has it been happening?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: About three weeks. First it was once a week, now it is almost every day. Today it came twice.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How long does each episode last? Does it settle with rest?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Five minutes or so, then it settles if I sit down. Today, um, I also felt sweaty, and I nearly fainted in the bank.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you have any other conditions? Do you smoke?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Sugar for six years and high pressure for ten. I smoke, about ten cigarettes a day. I have been trying to cut down.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What tablets do you take?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Metformin, five hundred twice a day, and a pressure tablet, um, amlodipine I think. And atorvastatin, but I forget it sometimes, maybe three days in a week.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Anyone in the family with heart problems?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: My brother had a heart attack at fifty. My father too, but he was older, seventy something.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Any allergies to medicines? I may need to give you a tablet that thins the blood.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: As far as I know, no allergies.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Let me check you now. Blood pressure is 152 over 94, pulse is 98, and oxygen is 96. Your heart sounds are normal and the chest is clear.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Doctor, is it my heart? I am very scared. My wife will panic.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: It could be angina, which is a heart problem from narrowed blood vessels, and we have to make sure it is not a heart attack in progress. I am not going to wait.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: What do you mean?

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: I will do an ECG right now in the next room, and we will send blood for a heart enzyme test. Chew this aspirin 300 milligrams now, please. Then I am sending you to the hospital emergency department by ambulance.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Right now? I have my car outside.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Yes, right now, and please do not drive yourself. Someone from here will go with you. Do not eat or drink anything until the hospital doctors see you.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Okay doctor. Please call my wife, her number is on my phone.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: We will. When you are discharged, come and see me in this clinic within a week, and bring the discharge papers.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Yes. Thank you, doctor.

gold.key: brother had a heart attack at fifty
sending you to the hospital emergency department
do not eat or drink anything
come and see me in this clinic within a week

notes: Red-flag consultation (urgent). The lift remark in turn 1 and the car and phone remarks in turns 21 and 23 are non-clinical and unlabelled. Turn 3 has both a symptom and a red flag (radiation to the left arm); turn 7 has a red flag (nearly fainted) and a symptom (sweaty). Smoking in turn 9 is not a gold category and is unlabelled. The patient's amlodipine is hedged (amlodipine I think) and adherence to atorvastatin is vague. Turn 13 my father too is a thin family-history statement. Turn 15 is a hedged no-allergies statement (labelled negated and uncertain). Turn 18 states a differential: a heart attack in progress is something the doctor wants to exclude, so it is labelled uncertain, not negated. Aspirin is NOT in the patient's own medicines, so it is a doctor-only medication_mention.
